summary: Azerbaijan lies in the Caucasus on the western shore of the Caspian Sea, is known for its oil resources and the nickname 'Land of Fire', and became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia)
ranking.description: Islam arrived with the Arab conquest in the 7th century, but the key to Azerbaijan becoming predominantly Shia was the Safavid dynasty, which began in Tabriz in 1501. The Safavid founder Ismail I wrote poetry in Azerbaijani Turkic and founded the state relying on the armies of Turkic tribes; he made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion and carried out conversion in what is now Azerbaijan and Iran, making Shia Islam the majority.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Sunnis are found mainly in the north bordering Dagestan in Russia and in places such as Zaqatala in the northwest, where Caucasian peoples such as the Lezgins and Avars are influenced by the Islamic traditions of the North Caucasus. The line between Shia and Sunni was blurred in the Soviet period, and with the recent influence of Turkey some young people have also converted to Sunni Islam.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christians are mainly Russian Orthodox (mostly ethnic Russians), together with the Caucasian Albanian Church tradition followed by the ancient Udi people of the Caucasus. Caucasian Albania accepted Christianity in the 4th century, and the Kish Church near Shaki is said to be one of the oldest churches in the Caucasus. Armenians were once an important Christian group, but most left after the Nagorno-Karabakh War of 1988-1994.

religion.background: In ancient times Azerbaijan was an important region of Zoroastrianism, and the natural gas flames near Baku were regarded as sacred fire, which is the origin of the nickname 'Land of Fire'. In the 4th century the kingdom of Caucasian Albania accepted Christianity, and after the Arab conquest in the 7th century Islam gradually replaced the older faiths. In the 16th century the Safavid dynasty made Shia Islam the state religion, forming the pattern of a predominantly Shia population. During Soviet rule from 1920 to 1991 atheism was promoted and a great many mosques were closed, so although Azerbaijan today is mainly Muslim, its society and politics are quite secular.

ranking.name: Azerbaijani
ranking.description: Azerbaijani belongs to the Oghuz branch of the Turkic language family and is close to Turkish; after the Seljuk Turks moved in in the 11th century, Turkic gradually replaced the local Iranian and Caucasian languages. The Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 divided Azerbaijan into a northern part (Russian) and a southern part (Persian), the north being today's Republic of Azerbaijan. The script has passed through the Arabic alphabet, the Latin alphabet in 1929 and the Cyrillic alphabet in 1939, and after independence in 1991 it was changed back to Latin; about 92 percent of the population speak it as a mother tongue.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian arrived after Russia conquered northern Azerbaijan in 1806-1828; at the end of the 19th century the Baku oil boom attracted large numbers of Russians and foreign capital, and in the Soviet period Russian was the language of administration, science and higher education. After independence the number of native Russian speakers declined as ethnic Russians emigrated, but in Baku many people still use Russian as a second language, and there are also schools taught in Russian.

language.history: In ancient times the Azerbaijan region used Iranian and Caucasian languages, and after the Seljuk Turks moved in in the 11th century Turkic became the main language; Azerbaijani literature had already appeared by the 13th and 14th centuries. In the 16th century Ismail I of the Safavid dynasty wrote poetry in Azerbaijani, but Persian remained the main language of the court and officialdom. After Russia took over the north in the 19th century Russian became the language of administration, and in the Soviet period of the 20th century the script was changed several times. After independence in 1991 Azerbaijani became the sole official language and switched to the Latin alphabet, and several million Azerbaijanis in northwestern Iran also still use the language.

ranking.name: Plov
ranking.description: Long-grain rice colored with saffron is steamed into loose grains and served with a separately cooked side dish stewed from chestnuts, dried apricots, raisins and lamb or chicken.
ranking.history: Azerbaijani plov was influenced by the cuisine of the Safavid Persian court, and differs from the Central Asian pilaf in which rice and meat are cooked together: the rice and the side dish are cooked separately and combined when served. Traditionally the bottom of the pot is lined with flatbread or an egg batter to make a crisp rice crust called 'gazmag'. There are more than 40 different versions across the country, and it is the main dish at weddings, Novruz (the spring equinox new year) and important banquets.

ranking.name: Dolma
ranking.description: Grape leaves or cabbage leaves are wrapped around ground lamb, rice and herbs and stewed; there are also versions stuffed into eggplants, tomatoes and green peppers, often served with garlic yogurt.
ranking.history: Wrapped and stuffed dishes have long been found in the Caucasus, Iran and the Ottoman region, and Azerbaijan, Armenia and Turkey all regard them as their own tradition. In 2017 UNESCO inscribed 'Dolma making and sharing tradition, a marker of cultural identity' on the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity for Azerbaijan, emphasizing its role in family gatherings and festivals. Azerbaijanis often say that how many kinds of dolma a household can make shows the skill of the housewife.

ranking.name: Gutab
ranking.description: Thin dough is filled with ground lamb, pumpkin or herbs, folded into a half-moon and dry-fried on a griddle, then brushed with butter and sprinkled with sumac when served.
ranking.history: Gutab is Azerbaijan's most common home snack, and the wild greens and herbs it uses reflect the rich plant life of the Caucasus mountains. During Novruz in spring, every household makes gutab with a green herb filling to celebrate the new year. There are also regional variations, such as a version filled with camel meat, regarded as a remnant of traditional caravan food.

ranking.name: Dushbara
ranking.description: Tiny dumplings filled with ground lamb are placed in a clear lamb-bone broth and seasoned with vinegar, garlic and dried mint, with a single spoonful holding several dumplings.
ranking.history: Dushbara belongs to the dumpling family of Central Asia and the Caucasus and is related to the pasta tradition that the Turkic peoples brought from the east. Azerbaijanis measure a housewife's skill by 'the smaller the dumpling the better', and it is said that the best dushbara fit a dozen or so in a single spoon. It often appears in winter and at family gatherings and is also a dish with which to show sincerity in hospitality.

ranking.name: Piti
ranking.description: A thick soup slowly stewed in a clay pot from lamb, chickpeas, chestnuts and saffron with lamb tail fat; the soup is drunk first and then the meat and beans are eaten.
ranking.history: Piti is the signature dish of the northern city of Shaki, which was the capital of the Shaki Khanate in the 18th century and also a merchant town on the Silk Road, where travelers ate this filling stew in caravanserais (such as the Shaki caravanserai still preserved today). The traditional way of eating is to tear bread into the soup first and then eat the meat and beans separately. In 2019 the Historic Centre of Sheki was inscribed on the World Heritage List, and piti also became the representative local dish for tourism.
